prompt: A router's uplink averages 80% utilisation. Traffic grows so it averages 90%. Using the simple M/M/1 model from the lesson, what happens to the average queueing delay? Keep mean service time fixed.

options.text: It rises by about 12%, in line with the extra load
options.explanation: Queueing delay is not linear in load. In the M/M/1 model the wait is the load divided by the spare capacity, which blows up as load approaches 100%.

options.text: It roughly doubles: from about 4 to about 9 packet times
options.explanation: Correct. At 80% load the wait is 0.8 / 0.2 = 4 packet times; at 90% it is 0.9 / 0.1 = 9. A 10-point rise in load more than doubles the wait.

options.text: It stays about the same, because the link still has 10% spare
options.explanation: Spare capacity on average doesn't mean no queue. Random bursts exceed the rate, and the closer to full, the longer each burst takes to drain.
At 90% load the M/M/1 mean wait is finite (9 packet times). At or above 1, this infinite-buffer model has no stationary finite mean; a real finite buffer instead drops traffic.

workedExample:
In the M/M/1 model the mean wait in the queue, measured in packet transmission times, depends only on the load:

```formula
W_q / T_s = ρ / (1 − ρ)
ρ = 0.8: 0.8 / 0.2 = 4
ρ = 0.9: 0.9 / 0.1 = 9
9 / 4 = 2.25
where
W_q: the mean time a packet waits in the queue before being sent
T_s: the mean service time: the time to transmit one packet
ρ: rho, the utilisation (traffic intensity): the fraction of the link's capacity in use, 0.8 or 0.9 here
In words: going from 80% to 90% load takes the average wait from 4 to 9 packet times, 2.25 times longer.
```

 Going to 95% would give 19, and to 99% gives 99. Actual delay depends on arrival and service distributions, buffers and scheduling; it can differ in either direction. This is why capacity planners upgrade links long before they hit 100%.
